Definition: from a compound of G575 and G3729; a starting-point, i.e. (figuratively) an opportunity:--occasion.
BiblicalUsage: An aphormē is a starting-point, a base of operations — the place an army launches from, or the excuse a person launches an argument from. Paul says sin took occasion by the commandment in Romans 7:8, and again in Romans 7:11 that sin deceived him by it and slew him; the law itself was good, but sin used it as its launching ground. The word cuts both ways: in 2 Corinthians 5:12 Paul gives the Corinthians an occasion to glory on his behalf, and in Galatians 5:13 he warns them not to use their liberty for an occasion to the flesh.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe this word exposes how sin works: it never attacks head-on if it can find a foothold instead. A good law, a real liberty, even a fair boast — any of them can become sin's starting-point once I hand it over. That is why Paul's answer is not to abandon the law or liberty, but to watch what I am launching from them — love serving one another, not the flesh serving itself.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
